newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak growing trade gap seen limiting cbank moves.
newsitem.headline: Slovak growing trade gap seen limiting cbank moves.

text.p: Slovakia's first quarter trade deficit should widen year-on-year, eliminating any room the central bank may have had for easing monetary policy, a Reuters survey of economists showed on Tuesday.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) is due to release official January-March foreign trade data on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik said last week preliminary figures showed a deficit of 15.9 billion crowns, and analysts said they expected little change in the data when published.
In first three months 1996, the trade balance had a shortfall of 15.44 billion crowns.

"The restrictive (monetary) policy finally showed the desired effect on the trade (balance) in the first two months of the year and we expect that favourable development to continue in the first quarter," Juraj Rencko, chief economic analyst at the Slovak Academy of Science, told Reuters.

"But it is too early to soften monetary policy since the NBS must be aware of the risk that more money in the economy could simply be used for consumption purposes and that would return trade balance to its previous problems," Rencko said.

Last week, central bank (NBS) Governor Vladimir Masar said the bank might ease its policy if the trade balance showed a positive trend and that the goal of a deficit of five percent of GDP appeared achievable.
Masar said the NBS could lower minimum reserve requirements or soften foreign exchange position curbs, implemented to curb foreign funds in local banking sector.
Some analysts said the government will most likely ease budgetary pressures by cutting some of its ambitious spending plans, giving the NBS room to manoeuvre with its monetary policy.
"To keep the trade balance at the planned track and achieve a deficit of five percent of GDP will really be a tough job," said Martin Barto, an analyst at ING Barings.

Charlie Robertson, an analyst from a London-based HILFE think-tank, said recent problems inside the ruling coalition, a forthcoming NATO membership referendum and 1998 general elections would make any budget cuts even more sensitive than usual.
"The Czechs had to do it recently, which is one year after the elections, but the Slovaks would have to cut budget spending one year before the polls which is much more difficult," Robertson said.
